{{short description|Type of argument}}
In [[argumentation theory]], an '''argumentation scheme''' or '''argument scheme''' is a template that represents a common type of [[argument]] used in ordinary [[conversation]]. Many different argumentation schemes have been identified. Each one has a name (for example, ''argument from effect to cause'') and presents a type of connection between ''[[premise]]s'' and a ''[[Logical consequence|conclusion]]'' in an argument, and this connection is expressed as a [[rule of inference]]. Argumentation schemes can include [[inference]]s based on different types of [[reasoning]]—[[deductive reasoning|deductive]], [[inductive reasoning|inductive]], [[abductive reasoning|abductive]], [[probabilistic reasoning|probabilistic]], etc.

The study of argumentation schemes (under various names) dates back to the time of [[Aristotle]], and today argumentation schemes are used for argument identification, argument analysis, argument evaluation, and argument invention.

Some basic features of argumentation schemes can be seen by examining the scheme called ''argument from effect to cause'', which has the form: "If ''A'' occurs, then ''B'' will (or might) occur, and in this case ''B'' occurred, so in this case ''A'' presumably occurred."<ref name="WaReMa2008"/>{{rp|170}} This scheme may apply, for example, when someone argues: "Presumably there was a fire, since there was smoke and if there is a fire then there will be smoke." This example looks like the [[formal fallacy]] of [[affirming the consequent]] ("If ''A'' is true then ''B'' is also true, and ''B'' is true, so ''A'' must be true"), but in this example the [[material conditional]] [[logical connective]] ("''A'' implies ''B''") in the formal fallacy does not account for exactly why the [[semantic relation]] between premises and conclusion in the example, namely [[causality]], may be reasonable ("fire causes smoke"), while not all [[Validity (logic)|formally valid]] [[Conditional proof|conditional]] premises are reasonable (such as in the valid ''[[modus ponens]]'' argument "If there is a cat then there is smoke, and there is a cat, so there must be smoke"). As in this example, argumentation schemes typically recognize a variety of [[semantic]] (or substantive) relations that inference rules in [[classical logic]] ignore.<ref>{{cite book |editor-last=Eemeren |editor-first=Frans H. van |editor-link=Frans H. van Eemeren |date=2001 |title=Crucial concepts in argumentation theory |location=Amsterdam |publisher=Amsterdam University Press |isbn=905356523X |oclc=49333598 }}</ref>{{rp|19}} More than one argumentation scheme may apply to the same argument; in this example, the more complex ''[[abductive reasoning|abductive]] argumentation scheme'' may also apply.

== Overview ==
Since the beginning of the discipline called [[rhetoric]],<ref name="AristotleRhetoric">{{cite journal |last=Braet |first=Antoine C. |date=March 2005 |title=The common topic in Aristotle's ''Rhetoric'': precursor of the argumentation scheme |journal=Argumentation |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=65–83 |doi=10.1007/s10503-005-2313-x |s2cid=145642868 |url=https://www.academia.edu/4465949 }} See also: {{cite book |author=[[Aristotle]] |title=On rhetoric: a theory of civic discourse |date=1991 |orig-year=4th century BCE |translator-last=Kennedy |translator-first=George A. |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford; New York |isbn=9780195064865 |oclc=22629945 }}</ref> the study of the types of [[argument]] has been a central issue.<ref>{{cite book |last1=van Eemeren |first1=Frans H. |author-link1=Frans H. van Eemeren |last2=Grootendorst |first2=Rob |author-link2=Rob Grootendorst |title=Argumentation, communication, and fallacies: a pragma-dialectical perspective |date=1992 |publisher=Lawrence Erlbaum Associates |location=Hillsdale |isbn=9780805810691 |oclc=24792772 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Toulmin |first1=Stephen |author-link1=Stephen Toulmin |last2=Rieke |first2=Richard D. |last3=Janik |first3=Allan |title=An introduction to reasoning. |date=1984 |orig-year=1979 |publisher=Macmillan Publishing Company |location=New York |isbn=9780024211606 |oclc=9783951 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Kienpointner |first1=Manfred |title=Alltagslogik: Struktur und Funktion von Argumentationsmustern |series=Problemata |volume=126 |date=1992 |publisher=Fromman-Holzboog |location=Stuttgart |isbn=9783772814624 |oclc=28724121 |lang=de }}</ref> Knowledge of types of argument allows a speaker to find the argument form that is most suitable to a specific subject matter and situation. For example, [[Argument from authority|arguments based on authority]] may be common in courts of law but not as frequent in a classroom discussion; [[Argument from analogy|arguments based on analogy]] are often effective in political discourse, but may be problematic in a scientific discussion.

The two interrelated goals of argument identification and analysis were the core of ancient [[dialectics]] (similar to [[debate]]), and specifically the branch called ''[[Topics (Aristotle)|topics]]''.<ref>{{cite book |author=[[Aristotle]] |title=Topics |date=1997 |orig-year=4th century BCE |translator-last=Smith |translator-first=Robin |series=Clarendon Aristotle series |publisher=Clarendon Press; Oxford University Press |location=Oxford; New York |isbn=9780198239420 |oclc=34411586 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author=[[Boethius]] |translator-last1=Stump |translator-first1=Eleonore |translator-link=Eleonore Stump |title=Boethius's De topicis differentiis |url=https://archive.org/details/boethiussdetopic00boet |url-access=registration |date=1978 |orig-year=522–23 BCE |publisher=Cornell University Press |location=Ithaca |isbn=9780801410673 |oclc=3414358 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Cicero |first1=Marcus Tullius |author-link=Cicero |translator-last=Reinhardt |translator-first=Tobias |translator-link=Tobias Reinhardt |title=Topica |date=2003 |orig-year=44 BCE |series=Oxford classical monographs |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford; New York |isbn=9780199263462 |oclc=54071435 }}</ref> In the 20th century, the ancient interest in types of arguments was revived in several [[academic discipline]]s, including [[education]], [[artificial intelligence]], [[legal philosophy]], and [[discourse analysis]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Eemeren |first1=Frans H. van |author-link1=Frans H. van Eemeren |last2=Grootendorst |first2=Rob |author-link2=Rob Grootendorst |last3=Snoeck Henkemans |first3=A. Francisca |display-authors=etal |date=1996 |title=Fundamentals of argumentation theory: a handbook of historical backgrounds and contemporary developments |url=https://archive.org/details/fundamentalsofar0000eeme |url-access=registration |location=Mahwah, NJ |publisher=Lawrence Erlbaum Associates |isbn=9780805818611 |oclc=33970847 |quote=It draws its data, assumptions, and methods from disciplines as disparate as formal logic and discourse analysis, linguistics and forensic science, philosophy and psychology, political science and education, sociology and law, and rhetoric and artificial intelligence.}}</ref>

The study of this ancient subject is mostly carried out today in the field of study called [[argumentation theory]] under the name of ''argumentation schemes''.<ref name="WaReMa2008">{{cite book |last1=Walton |first1=Douglas N. |last2=Reed |first2=Chris |last3=Macagno |first3=Fabrizio |title=Argumentation schemes |url=https://archive.org/details/argumentationsch0000walt |url-access=registration |date=2008 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge; New York |isbn=9780521897907 |oclc=181424052 |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511802034 }}</ref><ref name="Rigotti2019">{{cite book |last1=Rigotti |first1=Eddo |last2=Greco Morasso |first2=Sara |title=Inference in argumentation: a topics-based approach to argument schemes |date=2019 |series=Argumentation library |volume=34 |publisher=Springer |location=Cham |isbn=9783030045661 |oclc=1096259194 |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-04568-5 |s2cid=125412473 }}</ref>

An example of an argumentation scheme is the scheme for ''argument from position to know'' given below.<ref name="Walton2006">{{cite book |last=Walton |first=Douglas N. |author-link=Douglas N. Walton |date=2006 |title=Fundamentals of critical argumentation |series=Critical reasoning and argumentation |location=Cambridge, UK; New York |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=0521823196 |oclc=57434163 |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511807039 }}</ref>{{rp|86}}

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Argument from position to know
|-
| ''Premise'':
| ''a'' is in a position to know whether ''A'' is true or false.
|-
| ''Assertion premise'':
| ''a'' asserts that ''A'' is true ([or] false).
|-
| ''Conclusion'':
| ''A'' may plausibly be taken to be true ([or] false).
|-
|}

Following the usual convention in argumentation theory, arguments are given as a list of ''[[premise]]s'' followed by a single ''[[Logical consequence|conclusion]]''. The premises are the grounds given by the speaker or writer for the hearer or reader to accept the conclusion as true or as provisionally true (regarded as true for now). An argumentation scheme's definition is not itself an argument, but represents the structure of an argument of a certain type. The letters in the scheme, lower case ''a'' and upper case ''A'', need to be filled in if an argument is to be created from the scheme. Lower case ''a'' would be replaced by the name of a person and upper case ''A'' by a [[proposition]], which might be true or false.

Argumentation theorist [[Douglas N. Walton]] gives the following example of an argument that fits the ''argument from position to know'' scheme: "It looks as if this passer-by knows the streets, and she says that City Hall is over that way; therefore, let's go ahead and accept the conclusion that City Hall is that way."<ref name="Walton2006"/>{{rp|86}}

== History ==

Among 20th-century authors, [[Chaïm Perelman]] and [[Lucie Olbrechts-Tyteca]] may have been the first to write at length about argumentation schemes, which they called '''argumentative schemes'''<!--boldface per [[WP:R#PLA]]-->.<ref name="NewRhetoric">{{cite book |last1=Perelman |first1=Chaïm |author-link1=Chaïm Perelman |last2=Olbrechts-Tyteca |first2=Lucie |author-link2=Lucie Olbrechts-Tyteca |date=1969 |orig-year=1958 |title=The new rhetoric: a treatise on argumentation |url=https://archive.org/details/newrhetorictreat0000pere |url-access=registration |location=Notre Dame, IN |publisher=University of Notre Dame Press |oclc=21425 }}</ref>{{rp|9}}<ref name="Handbook2014"/>{{rp|19}} They present a long list of schemes together with explanation and examples in part three of ''The New Rhetoric'' (1958).<ref name="NewRhetoric"/> The argumentation schemes in ''The New Rhetoric'' are not described in terms of their logical structure, as in more recent scholarship on argumentation schemes; instead they are given prose descriptions. The structure of the arguments is, nevertheless, considered important by the authors.<ref name="NewRhetoric"/>{{rp|187}}

Perelman and Olbrechts-Tyteca also suggest a link between argumentation schemes and the ''loci'' (Latin) or ''[[Inventio#Topoi|topoi]]'' (Greek) of classical writers.<ref name="NewRhetoric"/>{{rp|190}} Both words, literally translated, mean "places" in their respective languages. ''Loci'' is a Latin translation of the Greek, ''topoi'', used by [[Aristotle]] in his work, ''[[Topics (Aristotle)|Topics]]'', about logical argument and reasoning. Perelman and Olbrechts-Tyteca explain ''loci'' as: "headings under which arguments can be classified".<ref name="NewRhetoric"/>{{rp|83}} And they write, "They are associated with a concern to help a speaker's inventive efforts and involve the grouping of relevant material, so that it can be easily found again when required."<ref name="NewRhetoric"/>{{rp|83}} While Aristotle's treatment of ''topoi'' is not the same as the modern treatment of argumentation schemes, it is reasonable to consider Aristotle as the first writer in the genre.<ref name="WaReMa2008"/>{{rp|267}}

The first contemporary writer to treat argumentation schemes in the way they are treated by current scholars and the way they are described in this article may have been Arthur Hastings in his 1962 Ph.D. dissertation.<ref>{{harvnb|Walton|Reed|Macagno|2008|p=3}}; {{cite thesis |type=Ph.D. thesis |last=Hastings |first=Arthur Claude |date=August 1962 |title=A reformulation of the modes of reasoning in argumentation |location=Evanston, IL |publisher=Northwestern University |oclc=18518112 |id={{ProQuest|288066554}} }} For extensive review of the history, see also {{harvnb|Walton|Reed|Macagno|2008}}, chapter 8 and section 7.3 for information about Hastings' treatment of argumentation schemes.</ref>

== Forms of inference ==

The study of argument in the field of argumentation theory since Perelman and Olbrechts-Tyteca's ''The New Rhetoric'' and [[Stephen Toulmin]]'s ''The Uses of Argument'',<ref>{{cite book |last=Toulmin |first=Stephen |author-link=Stephen Toulmin |date=2003 |orig-year=1958 |title=The uses of argument |url=https://archive.org/details/usesofargument0000toul_v7v3 |url-access=registration |edition=Updated |location=Cambridge, UK; New York |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=0521827485 |oclc=51607421 |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511840005 }}</ref> both first published in 1958, has been characterized by a recognition of the [[Defeasible reasoning|defeasible]], [[Non-monotonic logic|non-monotonic]] nature of most ordinary everyday arguments and reasoning.<ref name="Handbook2014">{{cite book |last1=Eemeren |first1=Frans H. van |author-link1=Frans H. van Eemeren |last2=Garssen |first2=Bart |last3=Krabbe |first3=Erik C. W. |last4=Snoeck Henkemans |first4=A. Francisca |last5=Verheij |first5=Bart |last6=Wagemans |first6=Jean H. M. |date=2014 |title=Handbook of argumentation theory |edition=Revised |location=New York |publisher=Springer |isbn=9789048194728 |oclc=871004444 |doi=10.1007/978-90-481-9473-5 }}</ref>{{rp|615}} A defeasible argument is one that can be defeated, and that defeat is achieved when new information is discovered that shows that there was a relevant exception to an argument in the presence of which the conclusion can no longer be accepted. A common example used in textbooks concerns [[Tweety]], a bird that may or may not fly:<ref name="Walton2006"/>{{rp|72–73}}

:(All) birds can fly;
:Tweety is a bird;
:Therefore, Tweety can fly.

This argument (with the addition of "All", which is shown in parentheses) has the form of a [[Syllogism|logical syllogism]] and is, therefore, valid. If the first two statements, the premises, are true, then the third statement, the conclusion, must also be true. However, if it is subsequently learned that Tweety is a penguin or has a broken wing, we can no longer conclude that Tweety can fly. In the context of [[deductive inference]], we would have to conclude that the first premise was simply false. Deductive [[inference rule]]s are not subject to exceptions. But there can be defeasible generalizations (defeasible inference rules). When we say that birds can fly, we mean that it is generally the case, subject to exceptions. We are justified in making the inference and accepting the conclusion that this particular bird can fly until we find out that an exception applies in this particular case.<ref name="Walton1996">{{cite book |last=Walton |first=Douglas N. |author-link=Douglas N. Walton |date=1996 |title=Argumentation schemes for presumptive reasoning |location=Mahwah, NJ |publisher=Lawrence Erlbaum Associates |isbn=9780805820713 |oclc=32704843 }}</ref>{{rp|21}}

In addition to deductive inference and defeasible inference, there is also [[Probability|probabilistic]] inference.<ref name="Walton2006"/>{{rp|65–69}} A probabilistic version of the generalization, "birds can fly", might be: "There is a 75% chance that a bird will be found to be able to fly" or "if something is a bird it probably can fly". The probabilistic version is also capable of being defeated (it is defeasible), but it includes the idea that the uncertainty might be quantifiable according to axioms of probability. (An exact number need not be attached as in the first example.<ref name="Walton2006"/>{{rp|67}})

In some theories, argumentation schemes are mostly schemes for arguments with defeasible inference although there could be schemes for specialized areas of discourse using other forms of inference, such as probability in the sciences.<ref name="WaReMa2008"/>{{rp|1–2}} For most or all everyday arguments, the schemes are defeasible.<ref>{{cite book |last=Walton |first=Douglas N. |author-link=Douglas N. Walton |date=2004 |chapter=Defeasible modus ponens arguments |title=Abductive reasoning |location=Tuscaloosa |publisher=University of Alabama Press |page=122 |isbn=0817314415 |oclc=55044871 }}</ref>

In other theories, the argumentation schemes are deductive or there is an attempt to interpret the schemes in a probabilistic way.<ref>For deductive and probabilistic, see sections 2.1 and 5 in: {{cite book |last=Lumer |first=Christoph |date=May 2011 |chapter=Argument schemes—an epistemological approach |editor-last=Zenker |editor-first=Frank |title=Argumentation: cognition & community: 9th biennial conference of the Ontario Society for the Study of Argumentation, May 18–21, 2011, University of Windsor |series=OSSA 9 |location=Windsor |publisher=Ontario Society for the Study of Argumentation |pages=1–32 |isbn=9780920233665 |oclc=843227451 |chapter-url=https://scholar.uwindsor.ca/ossaarchive/OSSA9/papersandcommentaries/17 }} For another probabilistic approach, see section 6 in: {{cite book |last1=Hahn |first1=Ulrike |last2=Oaksford |first2=Mike |last3=Harris |first3=Adam J. L. |date=2013 |chapter=Testimony and argument: a Bayesian perspective |editor-last=Zenker |editor-first=Frank |title=Bayesian argumentation: the practical side of probability |series=Synthese library |volume=362 |location=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer |pages=15–38 |isbn=9789400753563 |oclc=826657415 |doi=10.1007/978-94-007-5357-0_2 }} And: {{cite journal |last1=Hahn |first1=Ulrike |last2=Hornikx |first2=Jos |date=June 2016 |title=A normative framework for argument quality: argumentation schemes with a Bayesian foundation |journal=[[Synthese]] |volume=193 |issue=6 |pages=1833–1873 |doi=10.1007/s11229-015-0815-0 |s2cid=255062152 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/282545029 |hdl=2066/160400 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

== Examples ==

=== Argument from expert opinion ===
{{Main|Argument from authority}}
''Argument from expert opinion'' can be considered a sub-type of the ''argument from position to know'' presented at the beginning of the article. In this case, the person who is in a position to know is an expert who knows about some field.<ref name="WaReMaTables">Tables from {{harvnb|Walton|Reed|Macagno|2008|p=310}}.</ref>

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Argument from expert opinion<ref name="WaReMaTables"/>
|-
| ''Major premise'':
| Source ''E'' is an expert in subject domain ''S'' containing proposition ''A''.
|-
| ''Minor premise'':
| ''E'' asserts that proposition ''A'' is true (false).
|-
| ''Conclusion'':
| ''A'' is true (false).
|-
|}

=== Critical questions ===
The schemes of {{harvtxt|Walton|1996}} and {{harvtxt|Walton|Reed|Macagno|2008}} come with ''critical questions''. Critical questions are questions that could be asked to throw doubt on the argument's support for its conclusion. They are targeted toward key assumptions that, if true, make the argument acceptable. The reason these assumptions are presented in the form of questions is that these schemes are a part of a [[dialectical]] theory of argumentation.<ref name="WaReMa2008"/>{{rp|15}} An argument is dialectical when it is a back and forth of argument and [[rebuttal]] or questioning. This can be the case even when there is only one reasoner, presenting arguments, then seeking out new information or sources of doubt, or critically probing their own initial assumptions. Since everyday arguments are typically [[Defeasible reasoning|defeasible]], this is an approach to strengthening a case over time, testing each element of the case and discarding those parts that do not stand up to scrutiny.<ref>{{cite book |last=Rescher |first=Nicholas |author-link=Nicholas Rescher |date=1977 |title=Dialectics: a controversy-oriented approach to the theory of knowledge |url=https://archive.org/details/dialecticscontro0000resc |url-access=registration |location=Albany |publisher=State University of New York Press |isbn=087395372X |oclc=3034395 }}</ref>{{rp|47, 60}} The critical questions for ''argument from expert opinion'', given in {{harvtxt|Walton|Reed|Macagno|2008}}, are shown below.

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Critical questions for argument from expert opinion<ref name="WaReMaTables"/>
|-
| CQ1: ''Expertise question'':
| How credible is ''E ''as an expert source?
|-
| CQ2: ''Field question'':
| Is ''E'' an expert in the field that A is in?
|-
| CQ3: ''Opinion question'':
| What did ''E'' assert that implies ''A''?
|-
| CQ4: ''Trustworthiness question'':
| Is ''E'' personally reliable as a source?
|-
| CQ5: ''Consistency question'':
| Is ''A ''consistent with what other experts assert?
|-
| CQ6: ''Backup evidence question'':
| Is ''E'''s assertion based on evidence?
|-
|}

Another version of the scheme ''argument from expert opinion'', given in a textbook by {{harvtxt|Groarke|Tindale|Little|2013}}, does not include critical questions. Instead more of the key assumptions are included as additional premises of the argument.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Groarke |first1=Leo |author-link1=Leo Groarke |last2=Tindale |first2=Christopher W. |author-link2=Christopher Tindale |last3=Little |first3=J. Frederick |date=2013 |orig-year=1997 |title=Good reasoning matters!: a constructive approach to critical thinking |edition=5th |location=Don Mills, Ont.; Oxford |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=9780195445756 |oclc=799130281 }}</ref>

=== Argument from ignorance ===
{{Main|Argument from ignorance}}

''Argument from ignorance'' can be stated in a very informal way as, "if it were true, I would know it".<ref name="Walton1996"/>{{rp|112}} Walton gives the following example of an argument from ignorance: "The posted train schedule says that train 12 to Amsterdam stops at Haarlem and Amsterdam Central Station. We want to determine whether the train stops at Schipol. We can reason as follows: Since the schedule did not indicate that the train stops at Schipol, we can infer that it does not stop at Schipol."<ref name="Walton1996"/>{{rp|112}} Examples very much like this are well known in computer science discussions about the [[closed-world assumption]] for databases.{{Citation needed|date=April 2020}} One can assume that the train operating authority has a policy of maintaining a complete database of all of the stops and of publishing accurate schedules. In such cases it is fairly well assured that the information on the published schedule is correct even though it is possible for information to be missing from the database or not included in some particular schedule posting.

The scheme and its accompanying critical questions are shown below.<ref name="WaReMa2008"/>{{rp|327}}

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Argument from ignorance<ref name="WaReMaTables"/>
|-
| ''Major premise:''
| If ''A ''were true, then ''A'' would be known to be true.
|-
| ''Minor premise:''
| It is not the case that ''A'' is known to be true.
|-
| ''Conclusion:''
| Therefore, ''A'' is not true.
|-
|}

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Critical questions for argument from ignorance<ref name="WaReMaTables"/>
|-
| CQ1:
| How far along has the search for evidence progressed?
|-
| CQ2:
| Which side has the [[Burden of proof (philosophy)|burden of proof]] in the dialogue as a whole? In other words, what is the ultimate ''probandum'' [claim that is to be proved] and who is supposed to prove it?
|-
| CQ3:
| How strong does the proof need to be in order for this party to be successful in fulfilling the burden?
|-
|}

These critical questions, CQ2 and CQ3 especially, show the dialectical nature of the theory from which this scheme derives (that is, the scheme is based on a back and forth exchange between different parties). Two dialectical concerns are considered. It might be the case, as in some legal systems, that there is a presumption favoring a certain position—e.g., a [[presumption of innocence]] favoring the accused.<ref name="WaReMa2008"/>{{rp|98}} In that case, the [[Burden of proof (philosophy)|burden of proof]] is on the accuser, and it would not be proper to argue in the opposite direction: "If the accused were innocent I would have known about it; I don't know about it; therefore, the accused is not innocent." Even if it were a proper argument, the [[standard of proof]] in such a case (as asked in CQ3) is very high, [[beyond a reasonable doubt]], but the ''argument from ignorance'' alone might be very weak. When challenged, additional arguments would be needed to build a sufficiently strong case.<ref name="WaReMa2008"/>{{rp|35}}

See {{slink|Practical reason#In argumentation}} for a description of argumentation schemes for practical reasoning.

== Relation to fallacies ==

Many of the names of argumentation schemes may be familiar because of their history as names of [[fallacies]] and because of the history of the teaching of fallacies in [[critical thinking]] and [[informal logic]] courses. In his groundbreaking work, ''Fallacies'', [[Charles Leonard Hamblin|C. L. Hamblin]] challenged the idea that the traditional fallacies are always fallacious.<ref>See chapter 1 in: {{cite book |last=Hamblin |first=Charles Leonard |date=1993 |orig-year=1970 |title=Fallacies |series=Studies in critical thinking and informal logic |volume=1 |location=Newport News, VA |publisher=Vale Press |isbn=9780916475246 |oclc=29690976 }}</ref><ref name="Handbook2014"/>{{rp|25}} Subsequently, Walton described the fallacies as kinds of arguments; they can be used properly and provide support for conclusions, support which is, however, provisional and the arguments defeasible. When used improperly they can be fallacious.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Bench-Capon |first1=Trevor |author-link1=Trevor Bench-Capon |last2=Atkinson |first2=Katie |date=2010 |chapter=Argumentation schemes: from informal logic to computational models |editor1-last=Reed |editor1-first=Chris |editor2-last=Tindale |editor2-first=Christopher W. |editor2-link=Christopher Tindale |title=Dialectics, dialogue and argumentation: an examination of Douglas Walton's theories of reasoning and argument |series=Tributes |volume=12 |location=London |publisher=College Publications |pages=103–114 |isbn=9781848900059 |oclc=648095461 |chapter-url=https://www.csc.liv.ac.uk/~katie/waltonFest10.pdf }}</ref>

== Uses ==

Argumentation schemes are used for argument ''identification'', argument ''analysis'', argument ''evaluation'', and argument ''invention''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Janjua |first=Naeem Khalid |date=2014 |chapter=Argumentation life cycle |title=A defeasible logic programming-based framework to support argumentation in semantic web applications |series=Springer theses |location=Cham; New York |publisher=Springer |page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=Cxq4BAAAQBAJ&pg=PA33 33] |isbn=9783319039480 |oclc=895194510 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-03949-7 |hdl=20.500.11937/2073 }}</ref>

=== Argument identification ===
Argument identification is the identification of arguments in a text or spoken discourse. Many or most of the statements will not be arguments or parts of arguments. But some of those statements might look similar to arguments. Informal logicians have especially noted the similarity between words used to express arguments and those used to express explanations.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hansen |first1=Hans V. |last2=Walton |first2=Douglas N. |author-link2=Douglas N. Walton |date=January 2013 |title=Argument kinds and argument roles in the Ontario provincial election, 2011 |journal=Journal of Argumentation in Context |volume=2 |issue=2 |pages=226–258 |doi=10.1075/jaic.2.2.03han |ssrn=2334864 }} Section 6.5.</ref><ref name="Walton2019">{{cite book |last=Walton |first=Douglas N. |author-link=Douglas N. Walton |date=March 2019 |chapter=Argumentation schemes & their application in argument mining |editor-last=Blair |editor-first=J. Anthony |editor-link=J. Anthony Blair |title=Studies in critical thinking |series=Windsor Studies in Argumentation |volume=8 |location=Windsor |publisher=Centre for Research in Reasoning, Argumentation and Rhetoric, [[University of Windsor]] |pages=177–211 |isbn=9780920233863 |oclc=1125160111 |doi=10.22329/wsia.08.2019 |doi-access=free |chapter-url=https://windsor.scholarsportal.info/omp/index.php/wsia/catalog/view/106/106/1086-1 }}</ref> Words like "because" or "since" can be used to introduce reasons that justify argumentative positions, but they can also be used to introduce explanations: e.g., "something is the way it is ''because'' of the following explanation". Schemes may aid in argument identification because they describe factors that distinguish the argument type from other text. For example, an ''argument from expert opinion'' refers to an expert and a field of expertise, both of which could be identified in a text. Some schemes contain more easily distinguished characteristics than others.

==== Argument mining ====
[[Argument mining]] is the automatic identification of arguments in natural language using computing technology.<ref name="StedeSchneider">{{cite book |last1=Stede |first1=Manfred |last2=Schneider |first2=Jodi |title=Argumentation mining |series=Synthesis lectures on human language technologies |year=2018 |volume=40 |issue=2 |pages=1–191 |location=San Rafael, CA |publisher=Morgan & Claypool |isbn=9781681734590 |oclc=1083530996 |doi=10.2200/S00883ED1V01Y201811HLT040 }}</ref> It also includes some of the tasks of argument analysis.<ref name="StedeSchneider"/>{{rp|57}} The same benefits from the use of argumentation schemes as described above for identification and analysis are relevant to argument mining. Linguistic features that distinguish specific schemes can be used by computer algorithms to identify instances of those schemes and therefore automatically identify the arguments that are of those kinds.<ref name="StedeSchneider"/>{{rp|109–113}} Without the ability to notice such argumentative patterns, only features common to all arguments would be available. {{harvtxt|Feng|Hirst|2011}} proposed using argumentation schemes to automatically help fill in missing (implicit) premises in arguments, and they experimented with detecting instances of such schemes.<ref name="FengHirst">{{cite book |last1=Feng |first1=Vanessa Wei |last2=Hirst |first2=Graeme |date=June 2011 |chapter=Classifying arguments by scheme |title=Proceedings of the 49th annual meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics: human language technologies, 19 June 2011, Portland, Oregon, USA |series=ACL HLT |location=Stroudsburg, PA |publisher=[[Association for Computational Linguistics]] |pages=987–996 |isbn=9781932432879 |oclc=1150262180 |chapter-url=https://www.aclweb.org/anthology/P11-1099.pdf }}</ref> Similar work was done by Lawrence and Reed, and reported in 2016.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lawrence |first1=John |last2=Reed |first2=Chris |date=September 2016 |chapter=Argument mining using argumentation scheme structures |editor1-last=Baroni |editor1-first=Pietro |editor2-last=Gordon |editor2-first=Thomas F. |editor3-last=Scheffler |editor3-first=Tatjana |editor4-last=Stede |editor4-first=Manfred |title=Computational models of argument: proceedings of COMMA 2016 |series=Frontiers in artificial intelligence and applications |volume=287 |location=Amsterdam |publisher=IOS Press |pages=379–390 |isbn=9781614996859 |oclc=957551747 |doi=10.3233/978-1-61499-686-6-379 |s2cid=29571966 |chapter-url=http://www.johnlawrence.net/res/pubs/lawrence2016schemes.pdf }}</ref>

=== Argument analysis ===
Argument analysis is distinguishing the premises and conclusion of an argument and determining their relationships (such as whether they are ''linked'' or ''convergent''—see {{slink|Argument map#Key features}} for diagrams of such relationships), determining the form of inference, and making explicit any implicit premises or conclusions.<ref name="Walton2006"/>{{rp|138–171}} (These are the tasks of analysis from a [[logic]]al perspective. When discourse and rhetorical analyses are considered, there would be additional tasks.)

The logical analysis of arguments is especially made difficult by the presence of implicit elements.<ref name="NewRhetoric"/>{{rp|177}}<ref name="Walton2019"/>{{rp|208–9}} Their being implicit means that they are not present in the text (or spoken discourse) as statements; nevertheless, they are understood by the reader or hearer because of nonverbal elements or because of shared background knowledge from the social, cultural, or other shared, context. The implicit elements are also elements that are needed to make the argument [[wikt:cogent|cogent]]. Arguments containing implicit elements are called ''[[enthymeme]]s'', which is a term that was used by Aristotle in his works about dialectical reasoning and argument.<ref name="Handbook2014"/>{{rp|18}} If an argument appears to match a scheme but is missing some elements, the scheme could be used as a guide to determining what is implicit in the argument.<ref name="WaReMa2008"/>{{rp|189}}<ref name="FengHirst"/>{{rp|987}} An additional challenge with regard to this task could be that some schemes are easy to confuse. In Perelman and Olbrechts-Tyteca's concept of ''argumentative scheme'', different schemes could apply to the same argument depending on the interpretation of the argument or the argument could be described by multiple schemes.<ref name="NewRhetoric"/>{{rp|187–88}} Hansen and Walton also write that arguments may fit multiple schemes.<ref>{{harvnb|Hansen|Walton|2013}}, section 7.3.</ref>

=== Argument evaluation ===
Argument evaluation is the determination of the goodness of the argument: determining how good the argument is and whether, or with what reservations, it ought to be accepted. As mentioned above, in schemes accompanied by [[#Critical questions|critical questions]], a measure of the goodness of the argument is whether the critical questions can be appropriately answered. In other schemes, as in the example of the versions of ''argument from expert opinion'' in {{harvtxt|Groarke|Tindale|Little|2013}}, only good arguments fit the scheme because the criteria for goodness are included as premises,<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Hansen |first1=Hans V. |date=2019 |title=Argument scheme theory |conference=Third European conference on argumentation (ECA), June 24–June 27, 2019, [[Rijksuniversiteit Groningen]], The Netherlands: proceedings}}</ref> so if any one of the premises is false, the conclusion should not be accepted.

=== Argument invention ===
Argument invention is making new arguments to suit the occasion. As mentioned above, Perelman and Olbrechts-Tyteca attribute that use to the ''loci'' and ''topoi'' of the classical argumentation theorists.<ref name="NewRhetoric"/><ref name="Handbook2014"/>{{rp|20}} They form a catalog of argument types from which arguers may draw in constructing their arguments. With argumentation schemes described by their structure with single letter variables as placeholders, constructing such arguments is just a matter of filling in the placeholders. The arguer could use other words that convey the same meaning and embellish the argument in other ways.
